_comment: The flagship projects in the website's Featured section, in display order. Read by js/modules/flagships.js.
Each card shows: image, kicker, title, summary, up to three stats, the live link, and `links`. The `story` panels open under the cards from "How it was built".

Numbers that another project owns are never typed here. {atlas.cells}, {atlas.indicators}, {atlas.factors}, {atlas.datasets}, {atlas.presets}, {atlas.stations} and {atlas.resolution} are filled from data/livability-atlas.json, which scripts/fetch-atlas.js reads from the Atlas's live data bundle. A stat or a foot line whose number is missing is left out, never printed blank.

Images are 1200x750 WebP screenshots of each live app, under 250 KB. The crop cuts the map's own credits, so `image.credit` puts them back on the card. The screenshot is a mouse shortcut to the live link, hidden from screen readers because the card's main button says the same, so it needs no alt text.

flagships.title: Mapping thaw slumps across the Arctic
flagships.summary: A deep-learning system that finds retrogressive thaw slumps, the most dramatic form of abrupt permafrost thaw, in satellite imagery. I led it from the training data to a 32-GPU sweep of the circumpolar Arctic and an open, citable map.

story.title: Referee-proof by design
story.body: Leakage-free spatial splits, three-seed ensembles, object metrics corrected to the minimum mapping unit, and a full pre-launch audit. Benchmarked head-to-head against SAM2 and satellite foundation models up to 6.7B parameters: the purpose-built 30M-parameter UNet++ wins at a fraction of the compute.

story.title: Planetary-scale inference
story.body: An atomic shard-claim queue on cloud storage drove a self-healing fleet of 32 L4 GPUs through 41,567,572 tiles with exactly-once reconciliation, so every tile is accounted for. Docker-reproducible end to end, with a 338-test suite guarding the pipeline.

story.title: From pixels to open maps

figure.alt: A PlanetScope tile beside the same tile with the model's thaw-slump probability heatmap and decision-threshold contours
figure.caption: Model output on 2025 imagery, Northwest Territories, Canada

story.body: 19,068 high-confidence polygons across 529.7 km², drawn from 60,167 candidates at threshold 0.30, released as open vectors and cloud-optimized rasters. Builds on the open ARTS benchmark (Scientific Data) and deep-learning mapping in Remote Sensing of Environment.
story.foot: NSF Arctic Data Center · cloud-optimized GeoTIFF · open access

flagships.title: Scoring London by what matters to you
flagships.summary: An open-source tool for one question: where should I live? It scores every part of London by your own priorities, in your browser, and shows the data behind each score. I designed and built it, from the data pipeline to the web app.

stats.label: hex cells scored in your browser

story.title: Every build is checked before it ships
story.body: A Python pipeline fetches {atlas.datasets} public datasets, from police records to energy certificates and TfL timetables, aggregates them to an H3 hex grid, and writes a versioned data bundle. The bundle is published only if its QA report passes: structure, values, cross-checks between independent datasets, and known facts.
story.foot: H3 resolution {atlas.resolution} · versioned bundles · a QA gate on every build

story.title: The score is yours, and stays with you
story.body: Each score is a weighted sum that anyone can inspect, scored by the amount, never by rank. Hard limits grey out the cells that fail them, and a "No weak spots" mode stops a strong factor from hiding a weak one. Nothing goes to a server: the profile lives in the browser and in the link, and your own places never leave the device.
story.foot: {atlas.factors} factors · {atlas.presets} presets to start from · no server, no account

story.title: The answer first, the evidence one click away
story.body: The map shows the best areas. A hover gives a quick look, a click gives the reasons, and each measure opens to its dataset, date and licence. Travel times to your own places are estimated in the browser from a timetable matrix of {atlas.stations} stations.
story.foot: React · TypeScript · MapLibre · deck.gl · static hosting
